leadRef: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after Trump says he 'made the deal'
description: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang and markets rebound; CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9bn; OpenRouter drops three AI providers after leaked prompts; an Azure flaw exposes stored secrets; the RBI proposes a payments 'stop switch'; Z.ai ships a 750B looped model.

thirtySecond.p: CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler in stock for about $43.9bn, joining device and network security.
OpenRouter dropped three inference providers after Dragos's decoy credentials were stolen and used.
Indian banks would have to let customers switch off digital channels and would bear more fraud losses.

footerNote: Tuesday's deep beat, products, builders and open source: two looped models in four days (Z.ai's GLM-5.4 and Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini), Anthropic's agent that approves code, OpenAI and Cisco's open-source Shirudo, Ladybird's independent browser engine reaching alpha, and a warning from Dragos that 'zero retention' AI hosting can leak prompts.

stories.title: CrowdStrike agrees (23 Nov) to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing it at about $43.9bn, or $260.40 a share (1.135 CrowdStrike shares each), a 34% premium to Friday's close and the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record; close expected in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028; CrowdStrike shares fall about 9% to $208.97, Zscaler rises about 18% to $229.24
stories.h: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler for $43.9bn, the biggest cybersecurity deal ever
stories.ticker: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler for ~$43.9bn in stock; CRWD -9%, ZS +18%
stories.body:
CrowdStrike said on 23 Nov it will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal that values it at about $43.9bn, or $260.40 a share, a 34% premium to Friday's close; Zscaler holders get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares each (CrowdStrike SEC filing). It is the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record. CrowdStrike's Falcon protects devices and cloud workloads; Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange protects the network connections between them, a market CrowdStrike calls cybersecurity's largest. CrowdStrike expects about $1bn of revenue synergies and $500m of cost savings. Closing is expected in the second half of its fiscal year ending January 2028, subject to Zscaler shareholder and regulatory approval; Zscaler owes a $1.4bn break fee in some cases. Investors were cool: CrowdStrike fell about 9% to $208.97 and Zscaler rose about 18% to $229.24 (market data).

So what: banks that buy endpoint and zero-trust network security from these two vendors face a single supplier for both within about a year; review contract terms, exit clauses and concentration risk now.
stories.chip: Deal terms checked in CrowdStrike's SEC 8-K exhibit and SiliconANGLE's report (opened); share moves from market data
src: SiliconANGLE: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in record-setting $43.9B deal
Dark Reading: CrowdStrike makes AI security push with Zscaler deal
stories.short: CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9bn, a 34% premium and the largest cybersecurity takeover ever. It joins device and cloud protection with Zscaler's zero-trust network security. CrowdStrike shares fell about 9%; closing is expected in the second half of its fiscal 2028.

stat.label: value of the all-stock Zscaler deal

stories.title: OpenRouter removes inference providers Together AI, Phala and Novita (23 Nov) and revokes zero-data-retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after Dragos, which sent about two million prompts with canary credentials through AI services from July to November, found data from at least three providers exposed and its decoy AWS keys used by outsiders; Atlas Cloud withdraws its models voluntarily; OpenRouter says its own systems were not breached
stories.h: OpenRouter drops three AI providers after decoy prompts leaked to attackers
stories.ticker: OpenRouter drops Together AI, Phala, Novita after Dragos canary prompts leaked; 125 endpoints lose ZDR
stories.body:
Model marketplace OpenRouter removed three inference providers, Together AI, Phala and Novita, on 23 Nov and revoked zero-data-retention (ZDR) eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution, BleepingComputer reports. The trigger was a five-month test by industrial-security firm Dragos, which sent about two million prompts containing unique links and decoy credentials through widely used AI services. Dragos says data from at least three providers was exposed: its seeded prompts were later used to try to get into its test systems and canary AWS accounts. It also found resellers able to view and keep customer prompts with standard logging, and providers not honouring privacy settings. OpenRouter says its own systems were not breached. Atlas Cloud withdrew its models pending security testing; Together AI said an AI coding agent had exposed data.

So what: a 'zero retention' label on a model router is only as good as the hosts behind it; any bank sending customer or code data through third-party inference should map which providers actually serve its requests and assume secrets in prompts can leak.
stories.chip: Checked on Dragos's own write-up and BleepingComputer's report (both opened); provider statements not opened
src: Dragos: Three breaches, endless leaks: your AI supply chain needs canaries
BleepingComputer: OpenRouter drops AI providers over leaked prompts and secrets
The Hacker News: OpenRouter drops 3 providers after prompt theft
stories.short: OpenRouter removed Together AI, Phala and Novita and stripped zero-retention status from 125 endpoints after Dragos showed decoy credentials hidden in test prompts were stolen and used by outsiders. Dragos sent about two million prompts over five months. OpenRouter says its own systems were not breached.

stories.title: Microsoft warns customers (advisory MZK9-GH0) that a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers, found on 18 Nov and mitigated on 19 Nov, was exploited to read stored secrets (named values, identity-provider client secrets, subscription keys, management tokens) on instances not set up to best practice; Norwegian authorities link it to attacks on energy companies
stories.h: Azure API Management flaw exploited to steal customers' stored keys and secrets
stories.ticker: Azure API Management Classic flaw exploited to steal stored secrets; Microsoft mitigated 19 Nov
stories.body:
Microsoft told customers in an Azure Service Health advisory (MZK9-GH0) that a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal credentials stored in the service, BleepingComputer reports (23 Nov). Microsoft says it found the issue on 18 Nov and mitigated it on 19 Nov; instances not configured to its recommended practices exposed management functions to an unauthorised party. Possibly exposed: secrets in Named Values, identity-provider and OpenID Connect client secrets, subscription keys and management tokens. Norwegian authorities link the flaw to attacks on energy companies (SecurityWeek).

So what: banks publish many internal and partner APIs through APIM; if you run Classic tiers, rotate every stored secret and client credential now and check logs back to before 18 Nov.
stories.chip: Checked on BleepingComputer's report, which quotes Microsoft's customer advisory (opened); the advisory itself is sent to customers, not public
src: BleepingComputer: Microsoft Azure flaw exploited to steal customers' API credentials
SecurityWeek: Azure flaw exploited to target secrets at Norwegian energy firms
stories.short: Microsoft says attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to read stored secrets, including client secrets and subscription keys, on instances not set up to its best practices. It found the bug on 18 Nov and mitigated it a day later. Norway links it to attacks on energy firms.

stat.label: date Microsoft found the APIM flaw

stories.title: The RBI issues draft amendment directions (23 Nov) on 'Preventive Safeguards for Electronic Banking Transactions' for all bank types: customers would get a 'stop switch' to disable digital payment channels, set limits and block future debits, plus an optional Trusted Person Mechanism adding a second approval above a self-set threshold; failing to offer these, missing alerts, delayed complaint handling, system failures and staff or third-party collusion would count as bank negligence in fraud cases; comments due 14 Dec; separately SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank stay D-SIBs with unchanged buffers
stories.h: RBI proposes a 'stop switch' and widens when banks must pay for digital fraud
stories.ticker: RBI draft: customer 'stop switch', trusted-person approval; wider bank negligence in fraud; comments by 14 Dec
stories.body:
The Reserve Bank of India published draft amendments on 23 Nov to its responsible-business-conduct rules for every kind of bank, from commercial and small finance banks to co-operatives. Customers would get customer-induced controls, a so-called stop switch: the option to disable digital payment channels, set transaction limits and block future debits. A Trusted Person Mechanism would add an extra approval for transfers above a threshold the customer sets (ET BFSI). The RBI also widens what counts as bank negligence in fraudulent electronic transactions, which decides who bears the loss: not offering these controls, not applying required authentication, not sending alerts, delaying complaints, system malfunctions, security breaches and collusion by staff or third parties. It builds on June's customer-liability rules. Comments are due by 14 Dec. The same day the RBI kept SBI (0.80% extra CET1), HDFC Bank (0.40%) and ICICI Bank (0.20%) as systemically important banks.

So what: Indian banks would need to build channel kill-switches and a delegated-approval flow, and would carry more fraud losses where they fall short; product, fraud and legal teams should respond before 14 Dec.
stories.chip: Checked on the RBI's press releases (opened) and ET BFSI's summary of the draft (opened)
src: RBI: Draft Amendment Directions on Preventive Safeguards for Electronic Banking Transactions
ET BFSI: RBI expands definition of bank negligence in digital frauds
stories.short: India's central bank proposes letting customers switch off digital payment channels, cap transactions and add a trusted second approver for large transfers. Banks that fail to offer these, or miss alerts and complaints, would be treated as negligent and bear fraud losses. Comments are due by 14 December.

stat.label: deadline for comments on the RBI draft

stories.title: Z.ai (Zhipu) releases GLM-5.4 (23 Nov), its first looped transformer: the 750B-parameter model, retrained from the GLM-5 base, runs layers 27-54 twice with per-token gates and a shared KV cache, and Z.ai claims performance comparable to 2-3 trillion-parameter models; it is available on Z.ai's Coding Plan, weights to follow; in a 30B test the loop version raised AIME25 from 19.2 to 30.4 with about 10% more training compute
stories.h: China's Z.ai ships GLM-5.4, a 750B model that runs half its layers twice
stories.ticker: Z.ai GLM-5.4: 750B looped transformer, layers run twice; weights to follow
stories.body:
Z.ai (Zhipu) launched GLM-5.4 on 23 Nov, its first loop transformer: instead of using each layer once, the 750B-parameter model runs a block of shared layers (27 to 54) twice, making the network deeper without adding parameters. Z.ai retrained the GLM-5 base into a loop model, saying loop models trained from scratch did worse; per-token gates control how much each pass changes the result, and both passes share the KV cache so a 1M-token context stays affordable (The Decoder). Z.ai claims it performs like models of 2-3 trillion parameters and runs at 70-200 tokens a second. In a matched 30B test, looping lifted AIME25 from 19.2 to 30.4 with about 10% more training compute. It is on Z.ai's Coding Plan (not yet the regular API); weights are promised. Simon Willison found it comparable in quality to OpenAI and Anthropic models on his informal tests. It follows Thinking Machines' looped Inkling 2 Mini (20 Nov).

So what: two looped models in four days, one at frontier scale, suggest 'more compute per token' is becoming a standard way to get bigger-model quality from smaller weights; if the weights ship, expect it to undercut US closed models on price.
stories.chip: Architecture and claims checked on The Decoder's report of Z.ai's post and Simon Willison's hands-on note (both opened); Z.ai's own blog did not render; benchmarks are Z.ai's
src: The Decoder: Z.ai follows OpenAI into loop transformer territory with its new 750B flagship
Simon Willison: GLM-5.4, toward generalized coding with our first loop transformer
stories.short: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 is a 750-billion-parameter model that runs half its layers twice per token, a 'looped' design that adds depth without adding weights. Z.ai claims it matches models of 2-3 trillion parameters. It is on Z.ai's coding plan now, with open weights promised. Benchmarks are the company's own.

stories.title: US stocks rebound on 23 Nov as Huang returns: the Nasdaq Composite rises 6.5% to 24,089.56, the S&P 500 4.7% to 7,237.17 and the Dow 3.0% to 49,595.31; Nvidia +31.5% to $165.05, Micron +19%, Tesla +11.5%, AMD +7%; Anthropic slips 1.4% to $87.64; the Nikkei gains about 4% on 24 Nov; bitcoin touches $64,505
stories.h: Nasdaq jumps 6.5% and Nvidia 31% as Huang's return ends the sell-off streak
stories.body:
Markets reversed Friday's rout on Monday 23 Nov. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 24,089.56, up 6.5%; the S&P 500 rose 4.7% to 7,237.17 and the Dow 3.0% to 49,595.31 (market data). Nvidia jumped 31.5% to $165.05, adding close to $1tn in value, though it is still about 21% below a month ago (BBC). Micron rose 19%, Tesla 11.5% and AMD about 7%; Apple and Microsoft gained under 2%. The BBC says the rally began before the announcement and ended a week-long losing streak. Anthropic bucked it, slipping 1.4% to $87.64, close to its $83 IPO price. The US 10-year yield was flat at 4.92%. Asia followed on Tuesday: the Nikkei rose about 4% and the Kospi about 2.5%. Bitcoin touched $64,505 before easing to about $61,200 (Cointelegraph; market data).

So what: one personnel decision moved US equities by trillions in a day, which shows how concentrated AI risk has become; risk teams should treat single-name events at Nvidia as market-wide shocks in stress tests.
stories.chip: Index, Nvidia, Anthropic and Nikkei closes from Yahoo Finance market data (opened); stock moves and context from the BBC (opened); bitcoin high from Cointelegraph (opened)
src: BBC: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally
Cointelegraph: Bitcoin rebounds as Nvidia rally sparks $500M liquidations

stories.short: Wall Street recovered most of Friday's losses on Monday. The Nasdaq rose 6.5%, the S&P 500 4.7% and Nvidia 31.5% to $165.05 after Jensen Huang's reinstatement, adding about $1tn to its value. Micron and Tesla also jumped. Anthropic was an exception, slipping 1.4% to $87.64.

stories.title: Wells Fargo's updated customer agreement, effective 24 Nov, says use of any AI agent is 'at your own risk', part of a wider move by major US banks to bar third-party bots from logging into accounts and to shift liability for bot errors to customers (WIRED, 22 Nov); Reuters reports (23 Nov, exclusive) that some US banks are tightening AI-agent controls over concern that models can escape safeguards
stories.h: US banks shift AI-agent risk to customers as Wells Fargo's new terms start
stories.ticker: Wells Fargo terms from 24 Nov: AI agent use 'AT YOUR OWN RISK'; banks tighten agent controls
stories.body:
Wells Fargo's updated agreement with millions of customers takes effect on 24 Nov and says: 'Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK.' WIRED (22 Nov) reports that major US banks are banning third-party bots from logging into customer accounts and warning that costly bot mistakes are the customer's problem; Citi changed its terms in the same way last week. On 23 Nov Reuters reported, as an exclusive, that some US banks are tightening controls on AI agents over concern that models can escape safeguards (headline seen; article not opened). The moves follow Arizona's criminal probe into 'rogue AI agents' in banks (edition 149).

So what: the industry default is becoming 'block outside agents, push liability to the customer'; banks that want agent traffic will need an approved channel (scoped tokens, limits, logs) rather than screen-scraping logins.
stories.chip: Wells Fargo terms and the bank crackdown checked on WIRED's report (opened); the Reuters exclusive is a headline only
src: WIRED: Banks have had it up to here with your AI agent
American Banker: Banks are blocking external AI agents; is this sustainable?
stories.short: Wells Fargo's new customer terms, live from 24 November, say any AI agent use is at the customer's own risk. Major US banks are blocking third-party bots from logging in and shifting liability for bot mistakes to customers. Reuters reports some banks are tightening agent controls further.

stat.label: Wells Fargo AI-agent terms take effect

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship in beta (23 Nov): agents that review pull requests, push fixes and approve changes that a team's policy allows, building on Code Review; teams set where it runs and which changes need a person; eligible Claude Enterprise organisations can claim at least $10,000 in credits
stories.h: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents review, fix and approve code changes
stories.ticker: Anthropic Claude Ship beta: agents review, fix and auto-approve PRs within team policy
stories.body:
Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta on 23 Nov. It reviews pull requests, pushes fixes and approves the changes a team's policy allows, so routine changes can merge without a human approver; teams decide where it runs and which changes still need a person. Anthropic says that on the Claude Code team 'Claude writes most of our code' and it wanted everything after the PR to move as fast. Eligible Claude Enterprise organisations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits. TechCrunch notes that automatic approval, not review, is the new part: code review tools already existed.

So what: letting an AI approve its own kind of code moves accountability out of the four-eyes principle banks rely on; change-management and audit teams should decide now which change classes, if any, may be agent-approved.
stories.chip: Checked on Anthropic's announcement and TechCrunch's report (both opened)
stories.short: Anthropic's new Claude Ship, in beta, reviews pull requests, pushes fixes and can approve changes that a team's own policy allows, so routine code can merge without a human sign-off. Teams choose which changes still need a person. Enterprise customers can claim at least $10,000 in credits.

stories.title: The US Commerce Department says (23 Nov) it will add Singapore-based Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer whose former executive Alice Huang is alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset, to its Entity List after investigating for almost two years whether it helped get Nvidia chips to China; no effective date given; China denies she is a spy
stories.h: US moves to blacklist Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer at the centre of the spy scandal
stories.ticker: Commerce to add Singapore's Megaspeed to Entity List over suspected Nvidia chip diversion to China
stories.body:
The US Commerce Department announced on 23 Nov that it plans to add Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-centre developer and Nvidia customer, to its Entity List, which bars US trade without a licence (BBC). Commerce says it had investigated for almost two years whether Megaspeed helped move Nvidia's advanced chips to Chinese companies; it gave no effective date. Megaspeed's former CEO Alice Huang is alleged by US officials to be a Chinese intelligence asset who had an affair with Jensen Huang; China denies it and warns against a 'technological blockade'. Politicians have criticised Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not listing the company earlier (DW).

So what: the listing lands the same day Huang returns, so the export-control story continues even as the leadership one closes; banks financing Asian GPU clouds should screen for Megaspeed links and expect tighter end-use checks.
stories.chip: Checked on the BBC and DW (both opened); Commerce's notice not opened
src: BBC: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
DW: US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist
stories.short: The US Commerce Department will put Singapore's Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer whose former CEO is alleged to be a Chinese spy, on its trade blacklist. Commerce says it spent almost two years investigating whether the firm moved Nvidia chips into China. No start date was given.

stories.title: COP31 in Antalya ends on 22 Nov without a consensus cover decision for the first time since 2009, split over mentioning fossil fuels and carbon capture and over climate finance for developing countries; the EU, several Latin American and Pacific island states reject the presidency's text; countries do adopt a just-transition programme for fossil-fuel workers and a plan to assess adaptation progress
stories.h: COP31 climate talks end without a final agreement for the first time since 2009
stories.ticker: COP31 ends with no cover decision, first time since 2009; split on fossil fuels and finance
stories.body:
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday 22 Nov without consensus on a cover decision, the summit's main statement, for the first time since 2009 (Inside Climate News via Ars Technica). Countries split over whether to mention fossil fuels and carbon capture and over how much climate finance rich countries should provide; the EU, several Latin American countries and Pacific island states refused the presidency's text. Some decisions passed, including a programme to help workers and communities move away from fossil fuels and a plan to assess adaptation progress. A push for voluntary global electrification goals failed. More than 100,000 people attended.

So what: with no new global signal, climate policy moves back to national rules and trade measures such as the EU's carbon border tax; banks' transition plans should assume slower, more fragmented regulation.
stories.chip: Checked on Ars Technica's republication of Inside Climate News (opened); BBC coverage not opened
src: Ars Technica / Inside Climate News: COP31 ends in failure
BBC: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks
stories.short: The UN climate summit in Antalya ended on Sunday without its usual final statement, the first time since 2009. Countries split over mentioning fossil fuels and over money for poorer nations; the EU and others rejected the text. Smaller decisions on worker transition and adaptation did pass.

stat.label: last COP without a cover decision

stories.title: Ukraine says seven of its naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at the Benghazi naval base in Libya on 22 Nov and hit a Russian cargo ship it says carried weapons; both Libyan governments condemn the attack; the Kremlin warns of escalation; marine insurers widen war-risk zones
stories.h: Ukrainian drones sink a Russian warship in a Libyan port, far from the front
stories.ticker: Ukraine says naval drones sank Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi, Libya
stories.body:
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at the Benghazi naval base in Libya on Sunday 22 Nov, President Zelensky said; he named the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, and said seven naval drones were used. Ukraine says it also hit a Russian cargo ship it accuses of carrying weapons. Libya's rival governments in Tripoli and Benghazi both condemned the attack; the Kremlin warned of 'escalation of tensions in the region' (BBC). Insurance Business reports the strike widens the war-risk area for Mediterranean shipping. Zelensky has since called for four-way peace talks with Russia, Europe and the US.

So what: Ukraine can now strike Russian assets in the Mediterranean, which raises war-risk premiums and sanctions-screening stakes for shipping finance and trade-finance desks.
stories.chip: Checked on the BBC (opened); insurance angle from Insurance Business (not opened)
src: BBC: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says

stories.short: Ukraine says seven naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya, and hit a Russian cargo ship it says carried weapons. Both of Libya's rival governments condemned the strike and the Kremlin warned of escalation. Marine insurers are widening war-risk zones.

stories.title: Amazon agrees (23 Nov) to buy the technology behind Israeli startup Decart's Decart Optimization Stack (DOS) and hire its co-founders and AI team to speed inference and its Trainium chips; Decart has worked with Amazon on Trainium since 2025; reports put the deal at $7.5bn, which Amazon did not disclose
stories.h: Amazon buys Decart's inference-optimisation tech and team to speed up Trainium
stories.ticker: Amazon buys Decart's optimisation stack and team for Trainium; reported $7.5bn
stories.body:
Amazon said on 23 Nov it has agreed to buy the proprietary technology behind the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS) and bring Decart's co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf, with their researchers and engineers, to Amazon. Decart has worked with Amazon since 2025 on getting more performance out of Trainium by tuning software and hardware together; Amazon says the deal will speed inference and its custom chips for language, multimodal, agent and world models. Tech in Asia and others report the price at $7.5bn; Amazon did not state one. Decart is known for real-time world models such as Oasis.

So what: the cost of AI is increasingly set by software that squeezes chips, not just the chips; cheaper Trainium inference strengthens AWS's pitch to banks weighing Nvidia-based clouds.
stories.chip: Checked on Amazon's announcement (opened); the $7.5bn price is from headlines (Tech in Asia page did not render)
src: About Amazon: Amazon to purchase Decart's AI optimization technology

stories.short: Amazon is buying the technology behind Decart's optimisation stack and hiring its founders and team to make inference on its Trainium chips faster and cheaper. Decart has worked with Amazon since 2025. Reports put the price at $7.5bn; Amazon did not disclose one.

stories.title: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI say (23 Nov) teams of Gemini 4 agents found cheaper quantum algorithms and proved each correct in Lean: an 11.8x cost cut for a laser-fusion fuel calculation (error-corrected qubits from 5,650 to 4,338), about 8x for a light-sensitive molecule, 2.5x for the drug-metabolising enzyme cytochrome P450 and over 290x for a common arcsine subroutine
stories.h: DeepMind's Gemini agents find cheaper quantum algorithms and prove them in Lean
stories.ticker: DeepMind agents cut quantum-algorithm costs up to 290x, each proved in Lean
stories.body:
Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI said on 23 Nov that teams of Gemini 4 agents found more efficient quantum algorithms for problems in fusion, chemistry and drug design, and proved each result correct in the Lean theorem prover, because the circuits are too big to test on any computer today. The biggest gain: an 11.8x cheaper calculation for laser-driven fusion fuel, with memory down from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits. A light-sensitive molecule simulation became about 8x cheaper, the enzyme cytochrome P450 2.5x, and a widely used maths routine more than 290x (TNW). Agent teams shared verified ideas in a common notebook and 'met' every four hours to compare approaches.

So what: AI that makes quantum algorithms cheaper pulls forward the date when quantum machines matter, including for breaking today's encryption; keep post-quantum migration plans on schedule.
stories.chip: Checked on Google DeepMind's blog post and TNW's report (both opened)
src: Google DeepMind: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
TNW: DeepMind's AI agents found cheaper quantum algorithms, and proved them
stories.short: Google DeepMind says teams of Gemini 4 agents found cheaper quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems and proved each one correct in Lean. One fusion calculation became 11.8 times cheaper; a common maths routine more than 290 times cheaper. No quantum computer can run them yet.

stat.label: cost cut for a fusion-fuel calculation

stories.title: OpenAI and Cisco launch Shirudo (23 Nov), an open-source runtime that uses eBPF 'shields', which agents can write and test, to block exploitable code paths on running Linux systems until a patch ships; in a controlled test a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit against a live Elasticsearch service without a restart
stories.h: OpenAI and Cisco open-source Shirudo to shield unpatched Linux servers with AI
stories.ticker: OpenAI + Cisco open-source Shirudo: AI-written eBPF shields for unpatched Linux
stories.body:
OpenAI and Cisco launched Shirudo on 23 Nov, an open-source runtime that protects Linux systems while patches are tested and rolled out. It uses eBPF, small programs that run inside the operating system, to block the specific code path an exploit needs without taking the service offline. Agents can investigate a vulnerability, write a targeted 'shield' and test it against exploits and real traffic; security teams decide what is enforced and can watch a shield's effect before turning it on. In a controlled test a Codex-written shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service with no restart, OpenAI says.

So what: banks often wait weeks to patch core Linux systems; an open, auditable stop-gap layer is worth piloting, but treat agent-written kernel rules as code that needs review.
stories.chip: Checked on OpenAI's announcement (opened); Cisco's post not opened
src: OpenAI: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
SiliconANGLE: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo
stories.short: OpenAI and Cisco released Shirudo, open-source software that lets AI agents write small in-kernel rules to block an exploit on a running Linux server until a patch is ready. In OpenAI's test, a Codex-written shield stopped a Java4Shell attack on live Elasticsearch without a restart.

stat.label: restarts needed in OpenAI's Java4Shell test

stories.title: CFTC staff in the Divisions of Market Oversight and Clearing and Risk issue an advisory (23 Nov) that some crypto assets, including bitcoin, ether and stablecoins, can count toward the financial-resource (operating reserve) requirements of swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and clearinghouses, but not toward a separate liquidity requirement
stories.h: CFTC staff let exchanges count bitcoin and ether toward required reserves
stories.ticker: CFTC staff: crypto can count toward exchange reserves, not liquidity rule
stories.body:
Staff at the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in an advisory on 23 Nov that some crypto assets can count toward the financial resources that trading platforms and clearinghouses must hold to cover operating costs, but not toward a separate liquidity requirement (Reuters via CNA). It applies to swap execution facilities, designated contract markets and derivatives clearing organisations. Cointelegraph and The Block say bitcoin, ether and stablecoins are covered. It is a staff advisory, not a rule.

So what: it lets crypto-native venues use their own holdings to meet capital-like tests, which makes them more viable as regulated counterparties; banks clearing through them should check how much of a venue's cushion is now volatile crypto.
stories.chip: Checked on CNA's Reuters report (opened); the CFTC advisory itself not opened

stories.short: Staff at the US derivatives regulator say exchanges and clearinghouses can count some crypto, reportedly including bitcoin, ether and stablecoins, toward the reserves they must hold to cover operating costs, but not toward their separate liquidity requirement. It is a staff advisory, not a formal rule.

stories.title: CMS says (23 Nov) the third round of Medicare drug-price negotiations will save $9.2bn next year, a 45% net saving versus last year's prices, and for the first time includes Part B drugs given in doctors' offices; the figure excludes Part D manufacturer discounts
stories.h: Medicare's third round of drug-price talks to save $9.2bn, first with clinic drugs
stories.ticker: Medicare round 3 drug-price talks: $9.2bn savings, 45% net; first Part B drugs
stories.body:
The Trump administration said on 23 Nov that Medicare will save $9.2bn on drugs next year from its third round of price negotiations, a net saving of 45% against what it would have paid at last year's prices (STAT). It is the first round to include Part B drugs, given in doctors' offices, alongside retail Part D drugs. The estimate excludes discounts drugmakers already pay through the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program, which would shrink the figure.

So what: negotiated prices now reach infusion and specialist drugs, which hits the revenue models of large drugmakers and the lenders and investors exposed to them.
stories.chip: Checked on STAT's report (opened, partly paywalled); CMS release not opened
src: STAT: Medicare estimates $9.2 billion in savings from third round of negotiated drug prices
stories.short: Medicare says its third round of drug-price negotiations will save $9.2bn next year, 45% less than last year's prices would have cost. For the first time it covers drugs given in doctors' offices, not just pharmacy drugs. The figure leaves out discounts drugmakers already pay.

stories.title: Virginia AG Jay Jones and Oregon AG Dan Rayfield sue SpaceX and its subsidiaries (23 Nov) under state consumer and trade laws, alleging Grok's nudification feature produced sexual deepfakes, including of children, of millions of people earlier this year and that weak safeguards were a deliberate selling point
stories.h: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX over Grok-made sexual deepfakes, including of children
stories.ticker: Virginia, Oregon sue SpaceX over Grok nudification deepfakes
stories.body:
The attorneys general of Virginia (Jay Jones) and Oregon (Dan Rayfield) filed lawsuits on 23 Nov accusing SpaceX, which now owns xAI, and its subsidiaries of breaking state consumer and trade laws by letting Grok make deepfake nude images of millions of people earlier this year, including sexual images of children (CyberScoop). They allege SpaceX and Elon Musk repeatedly failed to block the nudification feature and that weak safeguards were a selling point to set Grok apart. Ars Technica says the states want a court order stopping Grok from generating such images.

So what: state consumer-protection law is becoming the route to hold AI makers liable for outputs; firms deploying image models need provable abuse filters, not policy statements.
stories.chip: Checked on CyberScoop's report (opened); the complaints not opened
src: CyberScoop: Virginia, Oregon hit SpaceX with fresh lawsuits over Grok-created CSAM
Ars Technica: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images
stories.short: Virginia and Oregon sued SpaceX, which owns xAI, alleging its Grok chatbot made nude deepfakes of millions of people earlier this year, including children, and that weak safeguards were a selling point. The states use consumer-protection law and want a court to stop such images.

Sierra closed a $1.75bn Series F led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed on 23 Nov, six months after its previous round (SiliconANGLE). Its product, Ghostwriter, builds AI agents from a prompt and uploaded files, checks the data and simulates conversations to find bugs before launch. Yahoo Finance reports a valuation of about $30bn, double six months ago.

So what: no-code agent builders for customer service are winning big budgets; banks buying them should test the simulated-conversation claims on their own complaint data.

stories.h: Apple Pay adds Tap to Share and debit top-ups as Walmart finally accepts it
stories.ticker: Apple Pay Tap to Share; Walmart completes US Apple Pay rollout
stories.body:
Apple is adding Tap to Share, an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone: a shopper taps a merchant's iPhone to share email, shipping address and loyalty details and watch the basket update before paying with Apple Pay. Customers of some banks can also reload debit cards inside Apple Wallet. Separately, Walmart and Sam's Club have completed their US rollout of Apple Pay, years after most big retailers (9to5Mac, 23 Nov).

So what: Walmart's switch removes the last big US holdout against tap-to-pay wallets; debit top-ups inside Wallet put Apple between banks and their cardholders.

stories.title: Ladybird, a browser with its own engine built from scratch rather than forked from Chromium, WebKit or Gecko, releases its first alpha for macOS and Linux (23 Nov) as a rolling channel with automatic updates, WebDriver and Firefox DevTools support; 1,350 points on Hacker News
stories.h: Ladybird, the first new independent browser engine in years, reaches alpha
stories.ticker: Ladybird browser alpha for macOS and Linux
stories.body:
Ladybird, a browser whose engine is written from the ground up rather than forked from Chromium, WebKit or Gecko, released its first alpha for macOS and Linux on 23 Nov, founder Andreas Kling wrote. It is a rolling channel with automatic updates; some sites will break and it makes no security promises yet. It supports WebDriver and the Firefox DevTools protocol so developers can test their sites. It was the top Hacker News story of the day (1,350 points).

So what: a fourth engine matters for web resilience; web teams can start adding it to test matrices.

stories.ticker: Korea's education minister resigns over AI cheating rules (NYT)
stories.body:
South Korea's education minister has resigned over the government's rules against AI-assisted cheating on the CSAT university entrance exam, The New York Times reports (22 Nov). On 16 Nov he told the National Assembly the ministry could not guarantee detecting cheating with AI devices such as smart glasses, and a complaint accusing him of dereliction of duty followed (Korea Herald). The ministry had already banned AI glasses and promised criminal charges and a three-year exam ban for offenders.

So what: wearable AI is breaking high-stakes testing, including the professional exams banks rely on for certification.

stories.update: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, citing input from senior US government officials; Trump says he 'made the deal'; shares jump 31.5%
stories.title: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstates Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director with immediate effect (23 Nov), less than two weeks after he resigned on 12 Nov over an affair with Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset; the board says it received input from senior US government officials and is confident he poses no national-security risk; Trump says he 'convinced' the board; the independent committee investigation continues and a new National Security and Export Control Committee is formed; Huang is due to testify to Congress in early December; Nvidia rises 31.5% to $165.05
stories.h: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after Trump says he 'made the deal'
stories.sub: Less than two weeks after his resignation over an alleged Chinese spy, the board brings Huang back, citing US government input; shares jump 31%.
stories.ticker: Nvidia board reinstates Huang as CEO; Trump says he 'made the deal'; NVDA +31.5% to $165.05
stories.body:
Nvidia's board voted unanimously on 23 Nov to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board member 'effective immediately', after meetings in which it was 'satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead' (Nvidia release). The board says it 'received input from senior levels of the United States government' and is confident his return 'poses no national security risk'. Huang resigned on 12 Nov after reports of affairs, including with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive US officials believe worked for Chinese intelligence; only last Tuesday the board said it did not intend to reinstate him (BBC). Trump said he 'convinced' the board and 'made the deal'. The independent directors' investigation 'will proceed to conclusion', and a new National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors will oversee trade compliance. Interim CEO Colette Kress stays CFO; Harvey Jones remains chair. Democrats accuse the administration of trading national security for market gains; Huang is due to testify to Congress in early December. Shares closed up 31.5% at $165.05.

So what: the leadership crisis is over but the open questions are not: the SEC accounting probe, the delayed 10-Q and Megaspeed all remain, now with the White House visibly involved in a private board's decision.
stories.brief:
The board's statement is unusual: it says outright that US government officials gave it input and that, on that basis, it is satisfied Huang poses no national-security risk. Six days earlier the same board had said it would not bring him back. Trump said on Monday that he had persuaded the board; Democrats, including Elizabeth Warren, want Congress to act, and Foreign Policy called it the biggest national-security scandal in US history.

Markets voted the other way. Nvidia added close to $1tn in value and took the Nasdaq up 6.5% (see the markets card). But the issues that drove last week's fall are still there: the SEC's reported look at Nvidia's accounting, the delayed quarterly filing, about $104bn of 2025 revenue booked through Singapore, and Megaspeed, which Commerce moved to blacklist the same day. The board's investigation continues, and a new committee will watch export compliance.

It comes on top of its pause of driverless freeway rides in five markets and its recall after California's DMV called freeway operation an 'imminent hazard'.

So what: weather and regulators both limit robotaxi availability during holiday travel.
